## What Is Covered in the Framework

### Part I — Historical Context
"La Campanella" traces its origins to Paganini's Violin Concerto No. 2 (1826), which Liszt heard performed in Paris in 1832 at age 20. He was so overwhelmed that he spent the next two decades refining his transcription through three distinct versions (1834, 1838, and the definitive 1851 edition in G-sharp minor). The final version was deliberately lightened in texture and moved to the upper register to achieve its signature shimmering, bell-like elegance.

### Part II — Complete Technical Evaluation
The piece presents five core technical challenges, each analyzed in detail:

| Challenge | Location | Why It Is Difficult |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Large Leaps** | Throughout; worst at mm. 30–32 | RH spans up to two octaves + a second within a sixteenth note; LH nearly three octaves at m. 101 |
| **Repeated Notes** | Opening and variation themes | Must ring cleanly like a bell; requires alternating fingers without tension |
| **4-5 Finger Trills** | mm. 80–83 | Weakest fingers share a tendon; must sustain while voicing a lower melody |
| **Chromatic Scales** | mm. 73+ | Must be feather-light and perfectly even at high speed |
| **Octaves & Chords** | Climax section | Requires wrist bounce endurance without locking up |

### Part III — Targeted Hanon Exercises
Eleven specific Hanon exercises are mapped directly to the piece's demands, including No. 46 (trills), No. 44–45 (repeated notes), No. 40 (chromatic scales), No. 53 (octave scales), No. 31 & 6 (extensions), and No. 39 & 41 (scales and arpeggios in G-sharp minor).

### Part IV — The 30-Day Daily Schedule
The plan is structured into four progressive weeks with a daily 2–2.5 hour session:

- **Week 1 (Days 1–7):** Anatomy — learn every section hands-separately at 50% tempo
- **Week 2 (Days 8–14):** Hands together at 60% tempo; prioritize accuracy over speed
- **Week 3 (Days 15–21):** Systematic tempo building with metronome; drill the three hardest passages
- **Week 4 (Days 22–30):** Performance preparation — endurance runs, musical shaping, and a final benchmark performance

### Part V — Essential Principles
The framework also covers injury prevention (never practice through tension), metronome discipline, memorization strategy, and the importance of listening to master recordings for musical inspiration.

---

Good luck — this is one of the great journeys in piano playing. Take it one day at a time.

The YouTube search uses only the **title and composer text** extracted by the AI — it builds a query like `"Franz Liszt La Campanella piano performance"` and picks the most-viewed result. It has no awareness of what is actually in the score file (key, tempo, edition, opus number, etc.).

## What "Reading the Sheet Music" Would Actually Require

**Reading the score visually (Optical Music Recognition)** means converting the uploaded PDF/image into machine-readable musical notation — detecting note pitches, rhythms, key signatures, and tempo markings. This is a specialized field called OMR. The current pipeline only runs `pdftotext` (which extracts embedded text, not notation) and then sends that to the LLM. A scanned score yields no text at all from `pdftotext`.

**Comparing that to a YouTube video** would then require audio fingerprinting or pitch analysis of the video's audio track — matching the detected musical content against what was found in the score.

This full pipeline (OMR → musical fingerprint → audio matching against YouTube) is research-grade work and not something that can be reliably built into a web app today.

| **AI-powered title disambiguation** | Before searching YouTube, send the extracted score text to the LLM and ask it to confirm the exact opus/catalogue number and edition — then use that in the query | Good for well-known repertoire |

Publishing to the Apple App Store requires converting the web app into a native iOS app. Here is an honest breakdown of what that involves and your realistic options.

---

## Why You Can't Submit Directly

The App Store only accepts native iOS apps (Swift/Objective-C) or cross-platform apps built with approved frameworks (React Native, Flutter, Capacitor, etc.). A web app hosted at a URL cannot be submitted as-is.

---

## Your Three Realistic Options

### Option 1 — Wrap the Web App with Capacitor (Fastest, ~1–2 weeks)

Capacitor is an open-source tool by Ionic that wraps an existing web app in a native iOS shell. Your React code stays exactly as it is — Capacitor adds a thin native layer around it.

| Step | What it involves |
|---|---|
| Install Capacitor | Add it to the project, configure the iOS target |
| Build the web app | Run `pnpm build` to generate the static output |
| Open in Xcode | Capacitor generates a native Xcode project automatically |
| Test on device | Run on a real iPhone via Xcode |
| Apple Developer account | Required — $99/year at [developer.apple.com](https://developer.apple.com) |
| Submit to App Store | Upload the build via Xcode or Transporter |

**Limitations:** App Store review team scrutinizes web-wrapper apps. Apps that are essentially just a website in a shell are frequently rejected under [App Store guideline 4.2](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/#minimum-functionality). You would need to ensure the app provides enough native-feeling functionality to pass review.

---

### Option 2 — Progressive Web App (PWA) — No App Store Needed
